Assignment 3: Image Colourization [50 Pt]¶

In this assignment, you will build models to perform image colourization. That is, given a greyscale image, we wish to predict the colour at each pixel. Image colourization is a difficult problem for many reasons, one of which being that it is ill-posed: for a single greyscale image, there can be multiple, equally valid colourings.

To keep the training time manageable we will use the CIFAR-10 data set, which consists of images of size 32x32 pixels. For most of the questions we will use a subset of the dataset. The data loading script is included with the notebook, and should download automatically the first time it is loaded.

We will be starting with a convolutional autoencoder and tweaking it along the way to improve our perforamnce. Then as a second part of the assignment we will compare the autoencoder approach to conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs).

In the process, you are expected to learn to:

  1. Clean and process the dataset and create greyscale images.
  2. Implement and modify an autoencoder architecture.
  3. Tune the hyperparameters of an autoencoder.
  4. Implement skip connections and other techniques to improve performance.
  5. Implement a cGAN and compare with an autoencoder.
  6. Improve on the cGAN by trying one of several techniques to enhance training.

This assignment is based on an assignment developed by Prof. Lisa Zhang and Prof. Jimmy Ba.

import os
import pickle
import sys
import tarfile

import numpy as np
from PIL import Image
from six.moves.urllib.request import urlretrieve


def get_file(fname, origin, untar=False, extract=False, archive_format="auto", cache_dir="data"):
    datadir = os.path.join(cache_dir)
    if not os.path.exists(datadir):
        os.makedirs(datadir)

    if untar:
        untar_fpath = os.path.join(datadir, fname)
        fpath = untar_fpath + ".tar.gz"
    else:
        fpath = os.path.join(datadir, fname)

    print("File path: %s" % fpath)
    if not os.path.exists(fpath):
        print("Downloading data from", origin)

        error_msg = "URL fetch failure on {}: {} -- {}"
        try:
            try:
                urlretrieve(origin, fpath)
            except URLError as e:
                raise Exception(error_msg.format(origin, e.errno, e.reason))
            except HTTPError as e:
                raise Exception(error_msg.format(origin, e.code, e.msg))
        except (Exception, KeyboardInterrupt) as e:
            if os.path.exists(fpath):
                os.remove(fpath)
            raise

    if untar:
        if not os.path.exists(untar_fpath):
            print("Extracting file.")
            with tarfile.open(fpath) as archive:
                archive.extractall(datadir)
        return untar_fpath

    if extract:
        _extract_archive(fpath, datadir, archive_format)

    return fpath


def load_batch(fpath, label_key="labels"):
    """Internal utility for parsing CIFAR data.
    # Arguments
        fpath: path the file to parse.
        label_key: key for label data in the retrieve
            dictionary.
    # Returns
        A tuple `(data, labels)`.
    """
    f = open(fpath, "rb")
    if sys.version_info < (3,):
        d = pickle.load(f)
    else:
        d = pickle.load(f, encoding="bytes")
        # decode utf8
        d_decoded = {}
        for k, v in d.items():
            d_decoded[k.decode("utf8")] = v
        d = d_decoded
    f.close()
    data = d["data"]
    labels = d[label_key]

    data = data.reshape(data.shape[0], 3, 32, 32)
    return data, labels


def load_cifar10(transpose=False):
    """Loads CIFAR10 dataset.
    # Returns
        Tuple of Numpy arrays: `(x_train, y_train), (x_test, y_test)`.
    """
    dirname = "cifar-10-batches-py"
    origin = "http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~kriz/cifar-10-python.tar.gz"
    path = get_file(dirname, origin=origin, untar=True)

    num_train_samples = 50000

    x_train = np.zeros((num_train_samples, 3, 32, 32), dtype="uint8")
    y_train = np.zeros((num_train_samples,), dtype="uint8")

    for i in range(1, 6):
        fpath = os.path.join(path, "data_batch_" + str(i))
        data, labels = load_batch(fpath)
        x_train[(i - 1) * 10000 : i * 10000, :, :, :] = data
        y_train[(i - 1) * 10000 : i * 10000] = labels

    fpath = os.path.join(path, "test_batch")
    x_test, y_test = load_batch(fpath)

    y_train = np.reshape(y_train, (len(y_train), 1))
    y_test = np.reshape(y_test, (len(y_test), 1))

    if transpose:
        x_train = x_train.transpose(0, 2, 3, 1)
        x_test = x_test.transpose(0, 2, 3, 1)
    return (x_train, y_train), (x_test, y_test)

Part (ii) [3pt EXPLORATORY]¶

Provided below is sample code to preproces the data to select only images of horses, which will help to simplify the goals of the assignment. The function also converts the colour images to greyscale to create our input data.

In [3]:
# select a single category.
HORSE_CATEGORY = 7

# convert colour images into greyscale
def process(xs, ys, max_pixel=256.0, downsize_input=False):
    """
    Pre-process CIFAR10 images by taking only the horse category,
    shuffling, and have colour values be bound between 0 and 1

    Args:
      xs: the colour RGB pixel values
      ys: the category labels
      max_pixel: maximum pixel value in the original data
    Returns:
      xs: value normalized and shuffled colour images
      grey: greyscale images, also normalized so values are between 0 and 1
    """
    xs = xs / max_pixel
    xs = xs[np.where(ys == HORSE_CATEGORY)[0], :, :, :]
    npr.shuffle(xs)

    grey = np.mean(xs, axis=1, keepdims=True)

    if downsize_input:
        downsize_module = nn.Sequential(
            nn.AvgPool2d(2),
            nn.AvgPool2d(2),
            nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2),
            nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2),
        )
        xs_downsized = downsize_module.forward(torch.from_numpy(xs).float())
        xs_downsized = xs_downsized.data.numpy()
        return (xs, xs_downsized)
    else:
        return (xs, grey)

# dataloader for batching samples

def get_batch(x, y, batch_size):
    """
    Generated that yields batches of data

    Args:
      x: input values
      y: output values
      batch_size: size of each batch
    Yields:
      batch_x: a batch of inputs of size at most batch_size
      batch_y: a batch of outputs of size at most batch_size
    """
    N = np.shape(x)[0]
    assert N == np.shape(y)[0]
    for i in range(0, N, batch_size):
        batch_x = x[i : i + batch_size, :, :, :]
        batch_y = y[i : i + batch_size, :, :, :]
        yield (batch_x, batch_y)

Part 2 Image Colourization as Regression [8 pt]¶

There are many ways to frame the problem of image colourization as a machine learning problem. One naive approach is to frame it as a regression problem, where we build a model to predict the RGB intensities at each pixel given the greyscale input. In this case, the outputs are continuous, and so squared error can be used to train the model.

In this section, you will be the training neural networks using cloud GPUs. Run the helper code and answer the questions that follow.

Helper Code¶

Regression Architecture

In [ ]:
class RegressionCNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, kernel, num_filters):
        # first call parent's initialization function
        super().__init__()
        padding = kernel // 2

        self.downconv1 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(1, num_filters, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(num_filters),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.MaxPool2d(2),)
        self.downconv2 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(num_filters, num_filters*2, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(num_filters*2),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.MaxPool2d(2),)

        self.rfconv = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(num_filters*2, num_filters*2, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(num_filters*2),
            nn.ReLU())

        self.upconv1 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(num_filters*2, num_filters, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(num_filters),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2),)
        self.upconv2 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(num_filters, 3, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(3),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2),)
        self.finalconv = nn.Conv2d(3, 3, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding)

    def forward(self, x):
        out = self.downconv1(x)
        out = self.downconv2(out)
        out = self.rfconv(out)
        out = self.upconv1(out)
        out = self.upconv2(out)
        out = self.finalconv(out)
        return out

Training code

In [5]:
class AttrDict(dict):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super(AttrDict, self).__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.__dict__ = self

def get_torch_vars(xs, ys, gpu=False):
    """
    Helper function to convert numpy arrays to pytorch tensors.
    If GPU is used, move the tensors to GPU.

    Args:
      xs (float numpy tenosor): greyscale input
      ys (int numpy tenosor): rgb as labels
      gpu (bool): whether to move pytorch tensor to GPU
    Returns:
      Variable(xs), Variable(ys)
    """
    xs = torch.from_numpy(xs).float()
    ys = torch.from_numpy(ys).float()
    if gpu:
        xs = xs.cuda()
        ys = ys.cuda()
    return Variable(xs), Variable(ys)

def train(args, gen=None):
  # Fix random seed
  npr.seed(args.seed)

  # Save dir (for CSV only)
  save_dir = os.path.join("outputs", args.experiment_name)
  os.makedirs(save_dir, exist_ok=True)

  # Model
  if gen is None:
      Net = globals()[args.model]
      gen = Net(args.kernel, args.num_filters)

  # Loss & optimizer
  criterion = nn.MSELoss()
  optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(gen.parameters(), lr=args.learn_rate)

  # Data
  print("Loading data...")
  (x_train, y_train), (x_test, y_test) = load_cifar10()

  print("Transforming data...")
  train_rgb, train_grey = process(x_train, y_train, downsize_input=args.downsize_input)
  test_rgb,  test_grey  = process(x_test,  y_test,  downsize_input=args.downsize_input)

  # Device
  if args.gpu:
      gen.cuda()

  print("Beginning training ...")

  train_losses = []  # average train loss per epoch
  csv_path = os.path.join(save_dir, "train_loss_every5.csv")
  # write header if not exists
  if not os.path.exists(csv_path):
      with open(csv_path, "w") as f:
          f.write("epoch,train_loss\n")

  last_images = None
  last_labels = None
  last_outputs = None

  for epoch in range(args.epochs):
      gen.train()
      losses = []

      for i, (xs, ys) in enumerate(get_batch(train_grey, train_rgb, args.batch_size)):
          images, labels = get_torch_vars(xs, ys, args.gpu)

          optimizer.zero_grad()
          outputs = gen(images)
          loss = criterion(outputs, labels)
          loss.backward()
          optimizer.step()

          losses.append(loss.item())

          # keep last batch for final visualization
          last_images, last_labels, last_outputs = images, labels, outputs

      # epoch average loss
      epoch_loss = float(np.mean(losses))
      train_losses.append(epoch_loss)

      # log every 5 epochs (no plotting here)
      if (epoch % 5) == 0:
          with open(csv_path, "a") as f:
              f.write(f"{epoch},{epoch_loss:.8f}\n")
          print(f"[epoch {epoch:03d}] train_loss={epoch_loss:.6f} (logged)")

  # Final: show sample grid + loss curve on screen (do not save)
  visual(last_images, last_labels, last_outputs,
          gpu=args.gpu, flag_torch=1, losses=train_losses)

  # (optional) save model weights
  torch.save(gen.state_dict(), os.path.join(save_dir, "regression_cnn.pt"))
  print("Training done. CSV logged. Loss curve displayed (not saved).")

  return gen

def visual(img_grey, img_real, img_fake, gpu=0, flag_torch=0, losses=None):
    """
    Show 5 grayscale inputs, 5 ground-truth RGBs, 5 predicted RGBs (top→bottom),
    and, if provided, also show the training loss curve. Nothing is saved to disk.
    """
    import numpy as np
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    # ----- sample grid -----
    if img_grey is not None and img_real is not None and img_fake is not None:
        if gpu:
            img_grey = img_grey.cpu().detach()
            img_real = img_real.cpu().detach()
            img_fake = img_fake.cpu().detach()
        if flag_torch:
            img_grey = img_grey.numpy()
            img_real = img_real.numpy()
            img_fake = img_fake.numpy()
        if flag_torch == 2:  # keep compatibility with your earlier branch
            img_real = np.transpose(img_real[:, :, :, :, :], [0, 4, 2, 3, 1]).squeeze()
            img_fake = np.transpose(img_fake[:, :, :, :, :], [0, 4, 2, 3, 1]).squeeze()

        # NCHW -> NHWC
        img_grey = np.transpose(img_grey[:5, :, :, :], [0, 2, 3, 1]).squeeze()
        img_real = np.transpose(img_real[:5, :, :, :], [0, 2, 3, 1])
        img_fake = np.transpose(img_fake[:5, :, :, :], [0, 2, 3, 1])

        plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
        for i in range(5):
            ax = plt.subplot(3, 5, i + 1)
            ax.imshow(img_grey[i], cmap='gray'); ax.axis("off")
            ax = plt.subplot(3, 5, i + 1 + 5)
            ax.imshow(np.clip(img_real[i], 0, 1)); ax.axis("off")
            ax = plt.subplot(3, 5, i + 1 + 10)
            ax.imshow(np.clip(img_fake[i], 0, 1)); ax.axis("off")
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()

    # ----- loss curve -----
    if losses is not None and len(losses) > 0:
        xs = np.arange(1, len(losses) + 1)
        plt.figure()
        plt.plot(xs, losses, marker='o')
        plt.xlabel('Epoch'); plt.ylabel('Train MSE'); plt.title('Training Loss Curve')
        plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
        plt.show()

Part (i) [2pt EXPLORATORY]¶

Describe the model RegressionCNN. How many convolution layers does it have? What are the filter sizes and number of filters at each layer?

In [ ]:
'''
The RegressionCNN has 6 convolution layers.
(downsampling -> downsampling -> receptive-field -> upsampling -> upsampling -> final)

The filter sizes and number of filters at each layer are:

downsampling conv layer 1: 3x3, 32 filters
downsampling conv layer 2: 3x3, 64 filters
receptive-field conv layer: 3x3, 64 filters
upsampling conv layer 1: 3x3, 64 filters
upsampling conv layer 2: 3x3, 32 filters
final conv layer: 3x3, 3 filters

'''

Part (ii) [3pt EXPLORATORY]¶

Run the regression training code (should run without errors). This will generate some images.

(a) How many epochs are we training the CNN model in the given setting?

(b) Name two other hyperparameters in args_dict that can influence the quality or speed of colourization results. Briefly describe how modifying each might affect the training process or the generated images.

(c) Looking at the generated colourized images, what qualitative differences do you notice between the predicted colours and the ground-truth images? Do you observe any systematic bias?

In [ ]:
'''
There are 51 epochs in the given setting.

Two hyperparamters that can influence the quality or speed of colourization are:
 1. Learning Rate:
  A larger learning rate may generate ocsillated colorization, and with more noise in the colorization, but it's faster.
  A smaller learning rate generates more stable colorization, but it converges slowlier, and need more epochs to train.

 2. Batch Size:
  The smaller batch size may lead to longer total training time, and more focus on regional features, so sharp colorization may happen, which is more bias than larger batch size.
  A larger batch size may generate smoother colors for images, but it use more computation.


Comparing with ground-truth color images, the generated color images:
  1. are less vibrant in colors
  2. have soft edges because colors spill at edges
  3. can't distinguish brown and green
  4. can't generate rare colors, like purple

The systematic bias are "brown-green bias" and low saturation, this may because the MSE averaging effecting, which cause the blurry images and fail to recover original image details.

'''

'''
When the epochs increases slightly (i.e. 51 -> 80), the generated color images show basic brown/green framework and basic edges, but still low saturation and color spills. Traninig loss decreases obviously.

When the epochs increases slightly (i.e. 80 -> 256), the generated color images show stronger brown/green distinguishment and more vibrant, but rare color like purple still gets averaged by MSE. Traninig loss decreases obviously.

When the epochs increases slightly (i.e. 256 -> 512), the generated color images show better details handling like color is closer to original image but not much improvement visually. Traninig loss drops a bit, almost remain the same.

When the epochs increases slightly (i.e. 51 -> 20), the generated color images show very blur and color spills situation, which is more like underfitting. Traninig increases a lot.

To sum up, the training loss decrease slowlier as larger epochs are trained, the generated images colorization is more smooth as larger epochs are trained but limits in improvement visually.

'''

Part (iv) [2pt MODEL]¶

Modify the autoencoder archeticture to use transposed convolution layers for the decoder portion. Ensure that the appropriate parameters are modified (e.g. input and output channels, padding) to accommodate this change. Train your model and present your best results. Hint1: Please check Pre3A_Autoencoder.ipynb for examples on how to use transposed convolution layers. Hint2: the output dimensions of upconv1 when using ConvTranspose2d for example should match the output of upconv1 when using Conv2d.

In [ ]:
class RegressionCNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, kernel, num_filters):
        # first call parent's initialization function
        super().__init__()
        padding = kernel // 2

        self.downconv1 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(1, num_filters, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding),                         # 32 -> 32
            nn.BatchNorm2d(num_filters),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.MaxPool2d(2),)                                                                       # 32 -> 16
        self.downconv2 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(num_filters, num_filters*2, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding),             # 16 -> 16
            nn.BatchNorm2d(num_filters*2),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.MaxPool2d(2),)                                                                       # 16 -> 8

        self.rfconv = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(num_filters*2, num_filters*2, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(num_filters*2),
            nn.ReLU())

# ======== COMPLETED ==========
        self.upconv1 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.ConvTranspose2d(num_filters*2, num_filters, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding, stride=2, output_padding=1),    # 8 -> 16
            nn.BatchNorm2d(num_filters),
            nn.ReLU()
        )

        self.upconv2 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.ConvTranspose2d(num_filters, 3, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding, stride=2, output_padding=1),                # 16 -> 32
            nn.BatchNorm2d(3),
            nn.ReLU()
        )
# =============================
        self.finalconv = nn.Conv2d(3, 3, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding)

    def forward(self, x):
        out = self.downconv1(x)
        out = self.downconv2(out)
        out = self.rfconv(out)
        out = self.upconv1(out)
        out = self.upconv2(out)
        out = self.finalconv(out)
        return out

Part 3 Skip Connections [5 pt]¶

A skip connection in a neural network is a connection which skips one or more layer and connects to a later layer. In this section we will be incorporating skip connections to improve on our model architecture.

Part (i) [2pt MODEL]¶

In this task, modify the original RegressionCNN class to implement a U-Net architecture by adding skip connections between the corresponding layers in the encoder and decoder (i.e., Add a skip connection from the first layer to the last, second layer to the second last, etc.). Specifically, the output of each downsampling block should be concatenated with the output of the corresponding upsampling block. For example, the input to upconv1 should be the concatenation of the output of rfconv and the output of downconv2. You will need to use torch.cat() to concatenate the feature maps along the channel dimension. Ensure the channel dimensions match after concatenation, possibly by adjusting the number of filters where necessary. The final convolution should have both the output of the previous layer and the initial greyscale input as input. Please complete the init and forward methods of the UNet class below. Hint: You will not need to update the downsampling part but you would need to update upsampling part and the final layer.

In [ ]:
#complete the code

class UNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, kernel, num_filters, num_colours=3, num_in_channels=1):
        super().__init__()

        # Useful parameters
        stride = 2
        padding = kernel // 2
        output_padding = 1

        ############### YOUR CODE GOES HERE ###############
        ###################################################

        # --------- Encoder (No Chnage) ---------
        self.downconv1 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(num_in_channels, num_filters, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding),                 # d1_in -> [B, 1, 32, 32]
            nn.BatchNorm2d(num_filters),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.MaxPool2d(2),)                                                               # d1_out -> [B, F, 16, 16]
        self.downconv2 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(num_filters, num_filters*2, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding),     # d2_in -> [B, 2F, 16, 16]
            nn.BatchNorm2d(num_filters*2),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.MaxPool2d(2),)                                                               # d2_out -> [B, 2F, 8, 8]

        # --------- Bottleneck ---------
        self.rfconv = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(num_filters*2, num_filters*2, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding),   # f -> [B, 2F, 8, 8]
            nn.BatchNorm2d(num_filters*2),
            nn.ReLU())

        # --------- Decoder ---------
        self.upconv1 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(num_filters*4, num_filters, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding),     # u1_in -> concat(d2_out, rf) -> [B, 2F+2F, 8, 8]
            nn.BatchNorm2d(num_filters),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2),)                                                   # u1_out -> [B, F, 16, 16]
        self.upconv2 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(num_filters*2, num_colours, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding),     # u2_in -> concat(d1_out, u1_out) -> [B, F+F, 16, 16]
            nn.BatchNorm2d(3),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2),)                                                   # u2_out -> [B, 3, 32, 32]
        self.finalconv = nn.Conv2d(num_in_channels+num_colours, num_colours, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding)
                                                                                            # final_in -> concat(x, u2_out) -> [B, 1+3, 32, 32]
                                                                                            # final_out -> [B, 3, 32, 32]



    def forward(self, x):
        ############### YOUR CODE GOES HERE ###############
        ###################################################
        d1 = self.downconv1(x)
        d2 = self.downconv2(d1)
        rf = self.rfconv(d2)
        u1_in = torch.cat([d2, rf], dim=1)
        u1 = self.upconv1(u1_in)
        u2_in = torch.cat([d1, u1], dim=1)
        u2 = self.upconv2(u2_in)
        final_in = torch.cat([u2, x], dim=1)
        out = self.finalconv(final_in)

        return out

In [ ]:
'''
PROVIDE YOUR ANSWER BELOW

Compared with my earlier AE , the U-Net consistently converged faster and to a lower (or at least more stable) MSE,
and produced visibly sharper results: object boundaries (mane/legs, horizon) are crisper and color bleed is reduced, with more coherent sky/grass hues.

Yes—skip connections improved the loss and the qualitative output.

Why skips help:

1. They enhance gradient flow (identity shortcuts), mitigating vanishing gradients and easing optimization.
2. They pass high-frequency encoder features (edges/textures) directly to the decoder, reducing blur.
3. Multi-scale fusion (shallow + deep features) improves localization while preserving semantics.




'''

PART B - Conditional GAN¶

In this second half of the assignment we will construct a conditional generative adversarial network for our image colourization task. This second half of the assignment should be started after the lecture on generative adversarial networks (GANs).

Part 1 Conditional GAN [10 Pt]¶

To start we will be modifying the previous sample code to construct and train a conditional GAN. Later you will have the opportunity to explore other modifications that can be made to our architecture to achieve the best results on image colourization model.

Part (i) [2pt MODEL]¶

Modify the below code to implement a generator. Then test to verify it works on the desired input (e.g., you could pass few inputs to your generator to verify it works with no errors). You should reuse one of your earlier autoencoder models from Part A here to act as a generator, when you do so, the architecture will be more like the pix2pix architecture (see https://phillipi.github.io/pix2pix/ for more details).

In [9]:
class Generator(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, kernel, num_filters, num_colours=3, num_in_channels=1):
        super().__init__()

        # Useful parameters
        stride = 2
        padding = kernel // 2
        output_padding = 1

        ############### YOUR CODE GOES HERE ###############
        ###################################################

        # --------- Encoder (No Chnage) ---------
        self.downconv1 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(num_in_channels, num_filters, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding),                 # d1_in -> [B, 1, 32, 32]
            nn.BatchNorm2d(num_filters),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.MaxPool2d(2),)                                                               # d1_out -> [B, F, 16, 16]
        self.downconv2 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(num_filters, num_filters*2, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding),     # d2_in -> [B, 2F, 16, 16]
            nn.BatchNorm2d(num_filters*2),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.MaxPool2d(2),)                                                               # d2_out -> [B, 2F, 8, 8]

        # --------- Bottleneck ---------
        self.rfconv = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(num_filters*2, num_filters*2, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding),   # f -> [B, 2F, 8, 8]
            nn.BatchNorm2d(num_filters*2),
            nn.ReLU())

        # --------- Decoder ---------
        self.upconv1 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(num_filters*4, num_filters, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding),     # u1_in -> concat(d2_out, rf) -> [B, 2F+2F, 8, 8]
            nn.BatchNorm2d(num_filters),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2),)                                                   # u1_out -> [B, F, 16, 16]
        self.upconv2 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(num_filters*2, num_colours, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding),     # u2_in -> concat(d1_out, u1_out) -> [B, F+F, 16, 16]
            nn.BatchNorm2d(num_colours),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2),)                                                   # u2_out -> [B, 3, 32, 32]
        self.finalconv = nn.Conv2d(num_in_channels+num_colours, num_colours, kernel_size=kernel, padding=padding)
                                                                                            # final_in -> concat(x, u2_out) -> [B, 1+3, 32, 32]
                                                                                            # final_out -> [B, 3, 32, 32]
        self.out_act = nn.Sigmoid()



    def forward(self, x):
        ############### YOUR CODE GOES HERE ###############
        ###################################################
        d1 = self.downconv1(x)
        d2 = self.downconv2(d1)
        rf = self.rfconv(d2)
        u1_in = torch.cat([d2, rf], dim=1)
        u1 = self.upconv1(u1_in)
        u2_in = torch.cat([d1, u1], dim=1)
        u2 = self.upconv2(u2_in)
        final_in = torch.cat([u2, x], dim=1)
        out = self.finalconv(final_in)

        return self.out_act(out)

Part (ii) [2pt MODEL]¶

Modify the below code to implement a discriminator. You will build a CNN-based discriminator that takes a color image and its corresponding grayscale image as inputs and outputs a single probability (real or fake).

Your discriminator should contain two convolutional layers that progressively increase the number of feature maps (num_filters → num_filters * 2), followed by a fully connected network for classification. You should also use LeakyReLU activations and dropout after each convolutional layer to improve stability.

In [10]:
# discriminator code

class Discriminator(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, kernel, num_filters, num_colours=3, num_in_channels=1):
        super().__init__()

        # Useful parameters
        stride = 2
        padding = kernel // 2
        output_padding = 1

        ############### YOUR CODE GOES HERE ###############
        ###################################################

        in_c = num_colours + num_in_channels  # 3 + 1 = 4
        nf   = num_filters

        # 2 x Conv blocks: nf -> 2*nf
        self.conv1 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(in_c, nf, kernel_size=kernel, stride=stride, padding=padding, bias=False),
            nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True),
            nn.Dropout2d(0.25),
        )
        self.conv2 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(nf, 2*nf, kernel_size=kernel, stride=stride, padding=padding, bias=False),
            nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True),
            nn.Dropout2d(0.25),
        )

        # GAP -> FC (small MLP) -> prob
        self.gap = nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1)
        self.fc  = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Flatten(),                      # [B, 2*nf, 1, 1] -> [B, 2*nf]
            nn.Linear(2*nf, 2*nf),
            nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True),
            nn.Dropout(0.5),
            nn.Linear(2*nf, 1),
            nn.Sigmoid(),
        )



    def forward(self, x, img_greyscale):

        ############### YOUR CODE GOES HERE ###############
        ###################################################
        inp = torch.cat([x, img_greyscale], dim=1)  # [B, 3+1, H, W]
        h = self.conv1(inp)
        h = self.conv2(h)
        h = self.gap(h)
        out = self.fc(h)                            # [B, 1]
        return out


        return out

Part (iii) [2pt MODEL]¶

Modify the provided training code to implement the training needed for a conditional GAN.

Your function should also plot the generator and discriminator losses over the training epochs on the same graph to visualize adversarial training dynamics.

In [11]:
class AttrDict(dict):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super(AttrDict, self).__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.__dict__ = self


def train(args, cnn=None):
    # Limit CPU threads to avoid oversubscription on shared machines
    torch.set_num_threads(5)

    # Reproducibility
    npr.seed(args.seed)

    # Output folder (not used for saving plots in this version)
    save_dir = "outputs/" + args.experiment_name
    if not os.path.exists(save_dir):
        os.makedirs(save_dir)

    # INPUT CHANNEL: grayscale unless downsized to RGB by your preprocessing
    num_in_channels = 1 if not args.downsize_input else 3

    # Load generator (your UNet/Generator)
    if cnn is None:
        Net = globals()[args.model]
        cnn = Net(args.kernel, args.num_filters, num_colours=3, num_in_channels=num_in_channels)

    # TODO: initialize the discriminator model (similar to how cnn is initialized)
    DiscNet = globals().get("Discriminator")
    assert DiscNet is not None, "Discriminator class must exist in globals()."
    discriminator = DiscNet(args.kernel, args.num_filters, num_colours=3, num_in_channels=num_in_channels)

    # LOSS FUNCTION
    # TODO: Use Binary Cross-Entropy loss
    # Note: this assumes your Discriminator ends with Sigmoid. If you switch to logits, use BCEWithLogitsLoss.
    criterion = nn.BCELoss()

    # TODO: Define separate optimizers for generator and discriminator
    lr = getattr(args, "lr", getattr(args, "learning_rate", 2e-4))
    betas = (0.5, 0.999)
    g_optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(cnn.parameters(), lr=lr, betas=betas)
    d_optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(discriminator.parameters(), lr=lr, betas=betas)

    # DATA
    print("Loading data...")
    (x_train, y_train), (x_test, y_test) = load_cifar10()

    print("Transforming data...")
    train_rgb, train_grey = process(x_train, y_train, downsize_input=args.downsize_input)
    test_rgb,  test_grey  = process(x_test,  y_test,  downsize_input=args.downsize_input)

    print("Beginning training ...")
    if args.gpu:
        cnn.cuda()
        discriminator.cuda()

    # Track epoch-averaged losses for both networks
    G_losses, D_losses = [], []
    last_batch_cache = None  # will store (img_grey, img_real, img_fake) from the last iteration

    for epoch in range(args.epochs):
        cnn.train()
        discriminator.train()

        epoch_g, epoch_d, nbatches = 0.0, 0.0, 0

        for xs, ys in get_batch(train_grey, train_rgb, args.batch_size):
            nbatches += 1

            # Get tensors: img_grey -> condition, img_real -> ground-truth RGB
            images, labels = get_torch_vars(xs, ys, args.gpu)   # images: [B,1,H,W], labels: [B,3,H,W]
            img_grey = images
            img_real = labels
            device = images.device

            # --------------------- Train Discriminator ---------------------
            d_optimizer.zero_grad()

            # TODO: Compute loss on real images
            D_real = discriminator(img_real, img_grey)
            real_labels = torch.ones_like(D_real, device=device)
            d_real_loss = criterion(D_real, real_labels)

            # TODO: Compute loss on fake images
            with torch.no_grad():
                img_fake_detached = cnn(img_grey)
            D_fake = discriminator(img_fake_detached, img_grey)
            fake_labels = torch.zeros_like(D_fake, device=device)
            d_fake_loss = criterion(D_fake, fake_labels)

            # TODO: Combine losses and update D
            d_loss = d_real_loss + d_fake_loss
            d_loss.backward()
            d_optimizer.step()

            # --------------------- Train Generator ------------------------
            g_optimizer.zero_grad()
            img_fake = cnn(img_grey)
            D_fake_for_g = discriminator(img_fake, img_grey)

            # TODO: Compute g_loss (generator tries to fool D → target ones)
            g_loss = criterion(D_fake_for_g, torch.ones_like(D_fake_for_g, device=device))
            g_loss.backward()
            g_optimizer.step()

            epoch_g += g_loss.item()
            epoch_d += d_loss.item()

            # cache last mini-batch for visualization after training
            last_batch_cache = (img_grey, img_real, img_fake)

        # Average losses over the epoch
        avg_g = epoch_g / max(1, nbatches)
        avg_d = epoch_d / max(1, nbatches)
        G_losses.append(avg_g)
        D_losses.append(avg_d)

        # >>> print every 5 epochs <<<
        if epoch % 5 == 0:
            print(f"[epoch {epoch:03d}] G_loss={avg_g:.6f}  D_loss={avg_d:.6f} (logged)")

    # Show loss curves (on the same figure, no saving)
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    plt.figure(figsize=(6,4))
    xs = list(range(len(G_losses)))
    plt.plot(xs, G_losses, label="Generator loss")
    plt.plot(xs, D_losses, label="Discriminator loss")
    plt.xlabel("Epoch")
    plt.ylabel("Loss")
    plt.title("cGAN Training Losses")
    plt.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    # Visualize several samples from the last batch using your provided visual()
    if last_batch_cache is not None:
        img_grey, img_real, img_fake = last_batch_cache
        visual(img_grey, img_real, img_fake, gpu=args.gpu, flag_torch=0, losses=None)

    return cnn

Part (vi) [2pt DISCUSSION]¶

There are two ways to implement the conditional GAN. The first is a standard conditional GAN for which the generator is a decoder with an input that is random noise with a conditional. The second is the pix2pix architecture where the generator is a UNet architecture with a greyscale image input.

Briefly describe the pros and cons of the two different approaches in regards to the image colourization task.

Limit your answer to no more than 100 words.

In [ ]:
'''
PROVIDE YOUR ANSWER BELOW

Standard cGAN (noise + condition)

 - Pros: Adds a “random knob” (noise), so the same grayscale photo can get multiple valid colorings—more creative.

 - Cons: Harder to train; can have weird colors or mode collapse. Without a reconstruction loss, colors can drift from the ground truth.

pix2pix (U-Net, grayscale → color)

 - Pros: Skip connections act like “coloring within the lines,” preserving edges and structure. It’s stable and sharp.

 - Cons: Usually one fixed coloring per input (low diversity), sometimes desaturated. It also needs paired and aligned training data.




'''

# Colorize 302 grayscale horse images with your trained UNet and save colourized.npz
import os, zipfile, numpy as np, torch, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from PIL import Image

# ---- your best model config (must match training) ----
args = {"gpu": True, "model": "UNet", "kernel": 3, "num_filters": 32, "experiment_name": "colourization_cnn"}

# ---- load trained UNet (state_dict saved by your train()) ----
def load_trained_unet(args):
    ckpt = os.path.join("outputs", args["experiment_name"], "regression_cnn.pt")
    dev  = "cuda" if (args["gpu"] and torch.cuda.is_available()) else "cpu"
    try:    G = UNet(args["kernel"], args["num_filters"])              # if UNet(kernel, num_filters)
    except TypeError:
            G = UNet(args["kernel"], args["num_filters"], 3, 1)        # fallback: (kernel, nf, num_colours, num_in_channels)
    G.load_state_dict(torch.load(ckpt, map_location=dev))
    return G.to(dev).eval(), dev

# ---- download & unzip grayscale set (uses your helper get_file) ----
RAW = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Sabaae/Dataset/main/grayimages.zip"
zip_path = get_file("grayimages.zip", origin=RAW, cache_dir="data")
root = "data/grayimages"; os.makedirs(root, exist_ok=True)
with zipfile.ZipFile(zip_path, "r") as z: z.extractall(root)

# collect exactly 302 images (handle nested /grayimages and duplicates)
scan_root = os.path.join(root, "grayimages") if os.path.isdir(os.path.join(root, "grayimages")) else root
all_paths = [os.path.join(dp,f) for dp,_,fs in os.walk(scan_root) for f in fs if f.lower().endswith((".png",".jpg",".jpeg"))]
uniq = {};
for p in all_paths:
    k = os.path.splitext(os.path.basename(p))[0]
    if k not in uniq: uniq[k] = p
paths = sorted(uniq.values())[:302]
assert len(paths) == 302, f"got {len(paths)}"

# ---- load model and run inference ----
G, dev = load_trained_unet(args)
outs = np.zeros((302,32,32,3), np.float32)
with torch.no_grad():
    for i, p in enumerate(paths):
        g = Image.open(p).convert("L").resize((32,32), Image.BILINEAR)
        x = torch.from_numpy(np.array(g, np.float32)/255.0)[None,None].to(dev)   # [1,1,32,32]
        y = G(x).clamp(0,1).cpu().numpy()[0].transpose(1,2,0).astype(np.float32) # (32,32,3)
        outs[i] = y

# ---- visualize first 10 pairs ----
plt.figure(figsize=(18,3.6))
for i in range(10):
    g = np.array(Image.open(paths[i]).convert("L").resize((32,32), Image.BILINEAR), np.float32)/255.0
    ax=plt.subplot(2,10,i+1); ax.imshow(g, cmap="gray"); ax.axis("off")
    ax=plt.subplot(2,10,10+i+1); ax.imshow(outs[i]); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# ---- save NPZ for grading ----
np.savez_compressed("colourized.npz", outs)
print("Saved colourized.npz", outs.shape, outs.dtype)

Summarize the qualitative performance of your best model on image colourization of new data and provide some reasons why it performs the way it does. Are there certain types of images on which your model works better than on others? Explain.

In [ ]:
'''
PROVIDE YOUR ANSWER BELOW
Summary:
The UNet produces plausible, coherent colorizations on many test horses—especially outdoor scenes with blue sky + green grass and mid-distance side-view horses,
showing good structure preservation from skip connections. However, colors are often desaturated, like muted backgrounds, with occasional loss of fine texture.

Why:
(1) Training with pixel loss (MSE) at 32×32 encourages averaging across many valid colors → muted results.
(2) No adversarial term to sharpen textures.
(3) Grayscale ambiguity (many colors map to similar luminance) cause safe, generic hues. The model performs worse on close-ups,
backlit/high-contrast shots, multiple/occluded horses, carts/riders, which may because it likely saw less during training.





'''

Part (ii) [2pt DISCUSSION]¶

The CIFAR10 images are 32x32 pixels in resolution. Do you believe that using similar images with a resolution of 256x256 would lead to better results. Why or why not?

Limit your answers to no more than 100 words.

In [ ]:
'''
PROVIDE YOUR ANSWER BELOW

It depends and potentially better with conditions.

If the dataset natively contains 256×256 pairs and we adapt the model (larger receptive fields, deeper G/D, PatchGAN, L1/perceptual losses), results can improve.
The improvements are finer edges, textures, and more faithful local color placement.

However, higher resolution isn’t a silver bullet. Colorization ambiguity is from semantic perspective, not purely pixel-limited.
Without stronger supervision and capacity, it just gets bigger blur. Training also becomes less stable and more data-hungry.
Also with limited paired data or unchanged objectives (e.g., pure RGB MSE), it may lead to overfitting or GAN collapse.

To sum up, only with adequate data, compute, and appropriately scaled architectures/losses, the performance imporves. Otherwise, it may not help or even hurt.


'''

Part (iii) [2pt DISCUSSION]¶

A colour space is a choice of mapping of colours into three-dimensional coordinates. Some colours could be close together in one colour space, but further apart in others. The RGB colour space is probably the most familiar to you, the model used in in our regression colourization example computes squared error in RGB colour space. But, most state of the art colourization models do not use RGB colour space. How could using the RGB colour space be problematic? Your answer should relate how human perception of colour is different than the squared distance. You may use the Wikipedia article on colour space to help you answer the question.

Limit your answers to no more than 100 words.

In [ ]:
'''
PROVIDE YOUR ANSWER BELOW

RGB color difference ≠ what human eyes feel. Two colors equally far apart in RGB may not look equally different to us.
By research, human eyes are more sensitive to changes in luminance and hue, however, RGB is not designed for human perception and its channels are correlated.
So optimizing RGB MSE makes models pick safe, grayish averages—numerically good, but not visually great.
To improve this, use perceptual color spaces (e.g., Lab with ΔE/CIEDE2000) or perceptual losses (e.g., VGG features).


'''

# ================== Task 1: incorporate a pretrained ResNet model =====================
"""
  I incoporate a ResNet-initialized pix2pix generator into my cGAN generator model.

  It uses a pretrained ResNet18 encoder (ImageNet) + a lightweight decoder with U-Net-style skips.

  It expects grayscale input [B,1,H,W] and outputs [B,3,H,W].

  The discriminator is the same without any change.
"""


import torch, torch.nn as nn
from torchvision.models import resnet18
from torchvision.models.resnet import BasicBlock

def _up(in_c, out_c):
    return nn.Sequential(
        nn.ConvTranspose2d(in_c, out_c, kernel_size=2, stride=2),
        nn.BatchNorm2d(out_c),
        nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
    )

class ResUNetGenerator(nn.Module):
    """
    Grayscale [B,1,H,W] --> Color [B,3,H,W]
    Encoder: ResNet18 (ImageNet) with conv1 adapted to 1 channel
    Decoder: U-Net-style with skip connections (enc0..enc4)
    """
    def __init__(self, freeze_encoder=True):
        super().__init__()
        r = resnet18(weights="IMAGENET1K_V1")   # torchvision>=0.13
        # adapt conv1 from RGB->grayscale by averaging RGB weights
        w = r.conv1.weight.data  # [64,3,7,7]
        r.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 64, kernel_size=7, stride=2, padding=3, bias=False)
        r.conv1.weight.data = w.mean(dim=1, keepdim=True)

        # encoder (keep layer names for easy freezing/unfreezing)
        self.enc0 = nn.Sequential(r.conv1, r.bn1, r.relu)     # [B,64,H/2,W/2]
        self.pool = r.maxpool                                  # -> [B,64,H/4,W/4]
        self.enc1 = r.layer1                                   # [B,64, H/4,W/4]
        self.enc2 = r.layer2                                   # [B,128,H/8,W/8]
        self.enc3 = r.layer3                                   # [B,256,H/16,W/16]
        self.enc4 = r.layer4                                   # [B,512,H/32,W/32]

        # decoder
        self.up4 = _up(512, 256); self.dec4 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(256+256, 256, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True))
        self.up3 = _up(256, 128); self.dec3 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(128+128, 128, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True))
        self.up2 = _up(128,  64); self.dec2 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d( 64+ 64,  64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True))
        self.up1 = _up( 64,  64); self.dec1 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d( 64+ 64,  64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(True))
        self.up0 = _up( 64,  32)
        self.out = nn.Conv2d(32, 3, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.act = nn.Sigmoid()  # use Tanh if you work in [-1,1]

        if freeze_encoder:
            for m in [self.enc0, self.enc1, self.enc2, self.enc3, self.enc4]:
                for p in m.parameters(): p.requires_grad = False

    def unfreeze_encoder(self):
        for m in [self.enc0, self.enc1, self.enc2, self.enc3, self.enc4]:
            for p in m.parameters(): p.requires_grad = True

    def forward(self, x):
        e0 = self.enc0(x)           # [B,64,H/2,W/2]
        p  = self.pool(e0)          # [B,64,H/4,W/4]
        e1 = self.enc1(p)           # [B,64,H/4,W/4]
        e2 = self.enc2(e1)          # [B,128,H/8,W/8]
        e3 = self.enc3(e2)          # [B,256,H/16,W/16]
        e4 = self.enc4(e3)          # [B,512,H/32,W/32]

        u4 = self.up4(e4); d4 = self.dec4(torch.cat([u4, e3], 1))
        u3 = self.up3(d4); d3 = self.dec3(torch.cat([u3, e2], 1))
        u2 = self.up2(d3); d2 = self.dec2(torch.cat([u2, e1], 1))
        u1 = self.up1(d2); d1 = self.dec1(torch.cat([u1, e0], 1))
        u0 = self.up0(d1)
        y  = self.act(self.out(u0))
        return y


# ------------------------- Training (cGAN with BCEWithLogits + L1) -------------------------
def train(args, gen=None):
    """ResUNetGenerator (pretrained ResNet18 encoder) + conditional D.
       Prints G/D losses every 5 epochs; plots only the last epoch's last batch;
       saves final checkpoints to outputs/<experiment_name>/{<model>.pt, Discriminator.pt}.
    """
    torch.set_num_threads(5)
    npr.seed(args.seed)

    # models
    if gen is None:
        gen = ResUNetGenerator(freeze_encoder=getattr(args, "freeze_encoder", True))
    disc = Discriminator(kernel=args.kernel, num_filters=args.num_filters,
                         num_colours=3, num_in_channels=(1 if not args.downsize_input else 3))

    # losses/optims
    adv_criterion = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()
    rec_criterion = nn.L1Loss()
    lrG = getattr(args, "lr_g", getattr(args, "learn_rate", 2e-4))
    lrD = getattr(args, "lr_d", lrG)
    g_opt = torch.optim.Adam(filter(lambda p: p.requires_grad, gen.parameters()), lr=lrG, betas=(0.5, 0.999))
    d_opt = torch.optim.Adam(disc.parameters(), lr=lrD, betas=(0.5, 0.999))

    # data
    print("Loading data...")
    (x_train, y_train), (x_test, y_test) = load_cifar10()
    print("Transforming data...")
    train_rgb, train_grey = process(x_train, y_train, downsize_input=args.downsize_input)

    # device
    if args.gpu:
        gen.cuda(); disc.cuda()

    print("Beginning training ...")
    l1_lambda  = getattr(args, "l1_lambda", 100.0)
    unfreeze_at = getattr(args, "unfreeze_at", 5)

    last_images = last_labels = last_outputs = None

    for epoch in range(args.epochs):
        gen.train(); disc.train()
        if getattr(args, "freeze_encoder", True) and epoch == unfreeze_at:
            gen.unfreeze_encoder()
            g_opt = torch.optim.Adam(filter(lambda p: p.requires_grad, gen.parameters()), lr=lrG, betas=(0.5, 0.999))

        ep_g = ep_d = 0.0; nb = 0
        for xs, ys in get_batch(train_grey, train_rgb, args.batch_size):
            nb += 1
            images, labels = get_torch_vars(xs, ys, args.gpu)
            x_gray, x_real = images, labels
            device = images.device

            # --- D ---
            d_opt.zero_grad()
            with torch.no_grad():
                x_fake = gen(x_gray)
            d_real = disc(x_real, x_gray)
            d_fake = disc(x_fake, x_gray)
            d_loss = adv_criterion(d_real, torch.ones_like(d_real, device=device)*0.9) + \
                     adv_criterion(d_fake, torch.zeros_like(d_fake, device=device))
            d_loss.backward(); d_opt.step()

            # --- G ---
            g_opt.zero_grad()
            x_fake = gen(x_gray)
            d_fake_for_g = disc(x_fake, x_gray)
            g_adv = adv_criterion(d_fake_for_g, torch.ones_like(d_fake_for_g, device=device))
            g_l1  = rec_criterion(x_fake, x_real)
            g_loss = g_adv + l1_lambda * g_l1
            g_loss.backward(); g_opt.step()

            ep_g += g_loss.item(); ep_d += d_loss.item()
            last_images, last_labels, last_outputs = x_gray, x_real, x_fake

        if epoch % 5 == 0:
            print(f"[epoch {epoch:03d}] G_loss={ep_g/max(1,nb):.6f}  D_loss={ep_d/max(1,nb):.6f} (logged)")

    # visualize only the last batch
    with torch.no_grad():
        visual(last_images, last_labels, last_outputs, gpu=args.gpu, flag_torch=1, losses=None)

    # ---- save final checkpoints (FIXED: use save_dir consistently) ----
    save_dir = os.path.join("outputs", getattr(args, "experiment_name", "exp"))
    os.makedirs(save_dir, exist_ok=True)
    gen_path  = os.path.join(save_dir, f"{getattr(args, 'model', 'Generator')}.pt")
    disc_path = os.path.join(save_dir, "Discriminator.pt")
    torch.save(gen.state_dict(), gen_path)
    torch.save(disc.state_dict(), disc_path)
    print(f"Saved final checkpoints:\n  G -> {gen_path}\n  D -> {disc_path}")

    return gen

# ------------------------- Model on Test Model -------------------------
def eval_on_test(args, batch_size=64):
    # 1) build model by name in args["model"]
    M = globals()[args["model"]]
    try:
        G = M(args.get("kernel",3), args.get("num_filters",64), num_colours=3,
              num_in_channels=(1 if not args.get("downsize_input",False) else 3))
    except TypeError:
        try: G = M(args.get("kernel",3), args.get("num_filters",64))
        except TypeError: G = M()  # e.g., ResUNetGenerator()

    # 2) load the checkpoint saved by train(): outputs/<experiment_name>/<model>.pt
    ckpt = os.path.join("outputs", args.get("experiment_name","exp"), f'{args["model"]}.pt')
    if not os.path.exists(ckpt):
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Checkpoint not found: {ckpt}")
    G.load_state_dict(torch.load(ckpt, map_location="cpu"))
    print(f"Loaded weights: {ckpt}")

    # 3) device & eval
    dev = "cuda" if (args.get("gpu",False) and torch.cuda.is_available()) else "cpu"
    G = G.to(dev).eval()

    # 4) data
    (_, _), (x_test, y_test) = load_cifar10()
    test_rgb, test_grey = process(x_test, y_test, downsize_input=args.get("downsize_input",False))

    # 5) metrics + show only last batch
    L1, MSE = nn.L1Loss(reduction="sum"), nn.MSELoss(reduction="sum")
    s1 = s2 = n = 0.0
    last_images = last_labels = last_outputs = None
    for xs, ys in get_batch(test_grey, test_rgb, batch_size):
        images, labels = get_torch_vars(xs, ys, gpu=(dev=="cuda"))
        preds = G(images)
        b = labels.size(0)
        s1 += L1(preds, labels).item()
        s2 += MSE(preds, labels).item()
        n  += b * labels.size(1) * labels.size(2) * labels.size(3)
        last_images, last_labels, last_outputs = images, labels, preds

    l1 = s1 / n
    mse = s2 / n
    psnr = 10.0 * math.log10(1.0 / max(mse, 1e-12))
    print(f"[TEST] L1={l1:.6f}  MSE={mse:.6f}  PSNR={psnr:.2f} dB")

    visual(last_images, last_labels, last_outputs, gpu=(dev=="cuda"), flag_torch=1, losses=None)

'''
My observation on incoporating ResNet:

Using a ResNet18-initialized U-Net generator with a conditional discriminator and BCE+L1 loss, my model produced noticeably sharper and more semantically plausible colorizations than the earlier
transpose-conv autoencoder.

Edges (mane/legs, horizon) were better preserved and color bleed reduced, consistent with skip connections reusing high-frequency details and the pretrained encoder supplying
object-level cues (horse/sky/grass).

A medium batch size (≈32) offered the best stability–detail trade-off; very large batches tended to desaturate, while very small batches introduced artifacts.

A key lesson was to match preprocessing with the output activation. I think to improve this, I can add perceptual/patch losses and scale to higher native resolutions.


'''

Assignment Grading Rubric¶

The grading of the assignment will be based on the following categories:

(1) 10 Pt - EXPLORATORY QUESTIONS These are basic questions that in most cases can be answered without requiring a fully working and trained neural network model. For example, data loading, processing and visualization, summary statistics, data exploration, model and training setup, etc.

(2) 10 Pt - MODEL Student has successfully implemented all the required neural network models and has demonstrated successful training of the model without any errors.

(3) 10 Pt - RESULT Students are evaluated based on the results achieved in comparison to the expected results of the assignment.

(4) 10 Pt - DISCUSSION QUESTIONS Student demonstrated understanding beyond the basic exploratory questions, can answer some of the more challenging questions, and provide arguments for their model selection decisions.

(5) 10 Pt - COMMUNICATION Student has provided a quality submission that is easy to read without too many unnecessary output statements that distract the reading of the document. The code has been well commented and all the answers are communicated clearly and concisely.

(6) 5 Pt - BONUS Student has completed the assignment and has taken on the challenging bonus tasks listed in PART C. The student has demonstrated a good understanding of all aspects of the assignment and has exceeded expectations for the assignment.
